_readme: Learning modules for Hopewick education pathways. All wording is original Hopewick text (no third-party text, scripts or worksheets reproduced). Schedule and Plus dates live in content-releases.json (kind: module). See docs/CONTENT-SOURCES.md.

modules.title: Cravings and triggers
modules.summary: What a craving is, what sets one off, and a few ways to ride one out.

cards.title: Cravings are common
cards.body: Cravings are a normal part of cutting down or stopping. Having one does not mean something has gone wrong, or that you will act on it.

cards.title: They rise and fall
cards.body: A craving tends to build, peak and then ease, often within half an hour or so. Knowing it will pass can make it easier to wait it out.

cards.title: Triggers set them off
cards.body: A trigger can be a place, a person, a time of day, a feeling, a smell, payday or an argument. Everyone's list is different.

cards.title: A quick HALT check
cards.body: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired. Any of these can make a craving louder. Checking in with HALT can point to what you actually need right now.

questions.q: A craving usually…
options: keeps getting stronger until you give in
questions.right: That's it. Cravings tend to move like a wave, even when it doesn't feel that way.
questions.wrong: Not quite, and that's okay. Cravings usually rise, peak and ease, even when they feel like they will last forever.

questions.q: Which of these can be a trigger?
questions.right: Yes. Triggers can be almost anything, which is why noticing your own matters.
questions.wrong: Close. All of these can be triggers, and everyone's mix is different.

cards.title: Delay
cards.body: Tell yourself you'll decide in 15 minutes. Set a timer. Often the urge has eased by then.

cards.title: Do something else
cards.body: Move your body, have a shower, make a cuppa, or do something with your hands.

cards.title: Breathe out slowly
cards.body: Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath for a minute or two.

cards.title: Reach out
cards.body: Text or call someone you trust. You don't have to explain everything.

cards.title: Surf the urge
cards.body: Notice where you feel the craving in your body and watch it change, without acting on it. The urge surfing tool walks you through it.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Think of a recent craving. What was going on just before it? Where were you, who were you with, and how were you feeling?

step.title: Make a 15-minute plan for my next craving
step.detail: Pick one thing to do for 15 minutes when a craving shows up, like a walk, a shower or texting someone.

sources.title: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention for Addictive Behaviors, 2nd edition (2021). Book reference, concepts only.

modules.title: Sleep basics
modules.summary: Simple habits that help sleep, and why sleep matters in recovery.

cards.title: Sleep and mood go together
cards.body: When sleep is poor, stress, low mood and cravings can all feel bigger. Small changes to sleep habits often help.

cards.title: Early recovery can be bumpy
cards.body: Sleep is often unsettled when someone cuts down or stops drinking or using. It usually settles, but it can take time.

cards.title: Alcohol and sleep
cards.body: Alcohol can make you drowsy, but it tends to break up sleep later in the night, so you wake less rested.

cards.title: Same wake-up time
cards.body: Getting up at about the same time every day, weekends included, helps set your body clock.

cards.title: A wind-down hour
cards.body: Dim the lights and put screens away for the last part of the evening. Do something calm.

cards.title: Go easy on stimulants
cards.body: Caffeine and nicotine can keep you awake for hours. Try to have them earlier in the day.

cards.title: If you can't sleep
cards.body: If you've been lying awake for a while, get up and do something quiet in dim light, then go back to bed when you feel sleepy.

questions.q: Which habit helps set your body clock?
options: Sleeping in on weekends to catch up
Getting up at about the same time each day
Scrolling in bed until you feel tired
questions.right: Yes. A steady wake-up time is one of the simplest things to try.
questions.wrong: Not quite. A steady wake-up time, weekends included, is what helps most here.

questions.q: Alcohol before bed…
options: can make you drowsy but tends to break up sleep later
questions.right: Right. It can feel like it helps, but sleep later in the night is often lighter.
questions.wrong: Not quite. Alcohol can help you nod off but usually breaks up sleep later in the night.

steps.title: A wind-down breath
steps.intro: Breathe in gently, then breathe out a little longer. Follow along for about a minute, or stop whenever you like.

phases.label: Breathe in
phases.text: Breathe in gently through your nose.

phases.label: Breathe out
phases.text: Breathe out slowly, a little longer than the in-breath.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: What's one thing that tends to get in the way of your sleep?

step.title: Pick a wake-up time for the next 7 days
step.detail: Choose a time you can stick to most days, and set an alarm for it.

modules.note: If sleep problems go on for more than a few weeks, or you are going through withdrawal, talk to your GP.

modules.title: Stress and anxiety basics
modules.summary: What stress and anxiety feel like in the body, and small things that can help.

cards.title: Stress
cards.body: Stress is how we react to pressure, like money worries, work or family. A bit of it is part of life. Too much for too long wears us down.

cards.title: Anxiety
cards.body: Anxiety is worry or fear that hangs around, or feels bigger than the situation. It is very common, and support helps.

cards.title: Your body's alarm
cards.body: A racing heart, tight chest, fast breathing or an upset stomach are signs your body's alarm system has switched on. It feels awful, and it does settle.

cards.title: Avoiding can keep it going
cards.body: Avoiding what makes us anxious brings quick relief, but over time the worry can grow. Small, steady steps towards things usually help more.

cards.title: Slow your breathing
cards.body: A longer out-breath can help your body settle.

cards.title: Move
cards.body: A short walk or some stretching can burn off some of the stress energy.

cards.title: Cut back on caffeine
cards.body: Caffeine can feel a lot like anxiety in the body.

cards.title: Talk to someone
cards.body: Saying it out loud to someone you trust can make it feel more manageable.

questions.q: Which can keep anxiety going over time?
options: Taking small steps towards what worries you
Avoiding everything that makes you anxious
questions.right: That's right. Avoiding brings quick relief, but it can make the worry grow.
questions.wrong: Not quite. Avoiding helps in the moment, but over time it can keep anxiety going.

questions.q: When might it be time to get more support?
options: When worry gets in the way of daily life for a few weeks
Only when things are an emergency
questions.right: Yes. You don't need to wait for a crisis. A GP is a good first step.
questions.wrong: You don't have to wait for an emergency. If worry is getting in the way for a few weeks, a GP or Beyond Blue can help.

steps.title: Slow breathing
steps.intro: Follow the prompts for about a minute. Breathe gently, without forcing it.

phases.label: Breathe out
phases.text: Breathe out slowly and let your shoulders drop.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Where do you notice stress or worry in your body? What usually helps, even a little?

step.title: Do a five-minute stress reset
step.detail: Take five minutes today for the stress reset tool, or a short walk.

modules.note: If you have chest pain or trouble breathing and you're not sure why, call 000.

sources.org: THIS WAY UP (St Vincent's Hospital Sydney)
sources.title: Learning hub

modules.title: Staying safer: harm reduction basics
modules.summary: Practical ways to lower risk, whether or not you're cutting down or stopping.

cards.title: Every safer step counts
cards.body: Harm reduction means lowering the risks of drinking or using, wherever you are at. You don't have to be stopping for it to matter.

cards.title: Alcohol guidelines
cards.body: Australian guidelines say healthy adults should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day, to reduce health risks. Less is safer.

cards.title: Tolerance drops after a break
cards.body: If you've had a break, even a short one, your body may not handle the amount it used to. That raises the risk of overdose.

cards.title: Mixing raises risk
cards.body: Mixing drugs, or drugs with alcohol or some medicines, can be much riskier than either alone.

cards.title: Don't use alone
cards.body: Let someone you trust know, so they can get help if something goes wrong.

cards.title: Start low, go slow
cards.body: Use a smaller amount first and wait, especially if anything is new or you've had a break.

cards.title: Naloxone
cards.body: Naloxone can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose. Through the Take Home Naloxone program it's free in Australia, with no prescription, from participating pharmacies and some health services. Always call 000 as well, because it wears off.

cards.title: In an emergency, call 000
cards.body: If someone is hard to wake, breathing strangely or not breathing, call 000 straight away. Paramedics are there to help, not to judge.

questions.q: After a break from using, your tolerance…
options: may be lower, which raises the risk of overdose
questions.right: Right. This is one of the most important safety points to know.
questions.wrong: Not quite. After a break, tolerance can drop, so the old amount can be riskier.

questions.q: Someone is hard to wake and breathing strangely. What's the first thing to do?
questions.right: Yes. Call 000 straight away.
questions.wrong: Please call 000 straight away. It's always okay to call.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Which one safer step could fit your life right now?

step.title: Save the National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline
step.detail: Put 1800 250 015 in your phone. It's free and confidential, 24 hours a day in most states.

sources.org: National Health and Medical Research Council
sources.title: Australian guidelines to reduce health risks from drinking alcohol (2020)
National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline

modules.title: Getting support in Australia
modules.summary: Free and low-cost places to turn, by phone, online or in person.

cards.title: Your GP
cards.body: A GP can talk through what's going on, check your physical health, and may set up a Mental Health Treatment Plan for Medicare-subsidised sessions with a psychologist or other mental health professional.

cards.title: National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline
cards.body: 1800 250 015. Free and confidential, 24 hours a day (in South Australia, 8.30 am to 10 pm). Connects you with the alcohol and drug service in your state or territory.

cards.title: Counselling Online
cards.body: Free alcohol and drug counselling by chat or email, any time, at counsellingonline.org.au. Also for family and friends.

cards.title: Beyond Blue
cards.body: 1300 22 4636 for support with anxiety, depression and stress, any time.

cards.title: 13YARN
cards.body: 13 92 76. For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, run by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crisis supporters, any time.

cards.title: In a crisis
cards.body: Lifeline 13 11 14 (any time), or call 000 if you or someone else is in danger.

questions.q: Who can set up a Mental Health Treatment Plan?
questions.right: Yes. Booking a longer GP appointment gives you time to talk it through.
questions.wrong: It's a GP. Booking a longer appointment helps.

questions.q: The National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline is…
options: free and confidential, 24 hours a day in most states
questions.right: That's right: 1800 250 015.
questions.wrong: It's free and confidential, 24 hours a day in most states: 1800 250 015. You don't need to be in an emergency.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Who is one person or service you could reach out to this week?

step.title: Save one support number in my phone
step.detail: Pick one: 1800 250 015 (alcohol and drugs), 13 11 14 (Lifeline) or your GP's number.

sources.title: National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline

modules.title: Thoughts, feelings and actions (CBT basics)
modules.summary: How thoughts, feelings and actions link up, and how to spot common thinking traps.

cards.title: The link
cards.body: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) looks at how what we think, feel and do affect each other. A situation sparks a thought, the thought shapes a feeling, and the feeling pulls us towards an action.

cards.title: Thoughts are not facts
cards.body: Thoughts are things our minds offer up, quickly and automatically. Some are helpful, some aren't. They're worth checking before we act on them.

cards.title: Noticing comes first
cards.body: You can't change what you don't notice. Catching a thought, and naming it, is the first skill.

cards.title: All-or-nothing
cards.body: Seeing things as total success or total failure. "I slipped once, so it's all ruined."

cards.title: Catastrophising
cards.body: Jumping to the worst possible outcome. "If I go to that party, it'll be a disaster."

cards.title: Mind reading
cards.body: Assuming you know what others think. "They think I'm hopeless."

cards.title: Should statements
cards.body: Rigid rules for yourself. "I should be over this by now."

cards.title: Labelling
cards.body: Turning one moment into who you are. "I'm a failure."

questions.q: "I had one drink, so I've blown it completely." Which thinking trap is this most like?
questions.right: Yes. One lapse is one moment, not the whole story.
questions.wrong: It's closest to all-or-nothing thinking. One lapse doesn't cancel out everything else.

questions.q: Thoughts are…
options: ideas our minds offer, worth checking
questions.right: Exactly.
questions.wrong: Thoughts can feel true, but they're ideas our minds offer. They're worth checking.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Write down a thought that's been on repeat lately. Does it look like any of the thinking traps?

step.title: Catch one thought today
step.detail: When you notice a strong feeling, pause and ask: what was I just thinking? Try the thought reframing tool if it helps.

sources.org: THIS WAY UP (St Vincent's Hospital Sydney)
sources.title: Learning hub

modules.title: Unhooking from difficult thoughts (ACT basics)
modules.summary: Step back from sticky thoughts and steady yourself when feelings run high.

steps.title: A different way to relate to thoughts

cards.title: What ACT is
cards.body: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) helps people make room for hard thoughts and feelings, so they have less pull, and put more energy into what matters to them. These ideas are inspired by the work of Dr Russ Harris, author of The Happiness Trap. The wording here is Hopewick's own.

cards.title: Getting hooked
cards.body: Sometimes a thought grabs hold and we act as if it's an order or the whole truth. "I can't cope" can feel like a fact, not a thought.

cards.title: Unhooking
cards.body: Unhooking means noticing a thought as a thought: words and pictures passing through your mind. You don't have to argue with it or obey it.

cards.title: Dropping anchor
cards.body: When feelings are like a storm, an anchor doesn't stop the storm. It holds you steady until it passes. You notice what's here, feel your body, and come back to the room around you.

steps.title: Try unhooking
steps.intro: Type a thought that's been bothering you. Hopewick will show it back to you in a way that gives you a bit of space from it. Nothing you type here is saved.
steps.prompt: A thought that's been bothering me

steps.title: Drop anchor (about a minute)
steps.intro: Follow each prompt at your own pace. You can pause or stop at any time.

phases.label: Notice
phases.text: Notice what's here right now. Silently name it, like "here's worry" or "here's a craving".

phases.label: Feel your body
phases.text: Press your feet into the floor. Sit up a little. Slowly press your fingertips together.

phases.label: Look around
phases.text: Look around and notice five things you can see. Then notice two things you can hear.

phases.label: Both are here
phases.text: The hard feelings are here, and so is your body, and so is this room around you.

phases.label: Next step
phases.text: What's one small thing you could do next, that matters to you?

questions.q: Unhooking from a thought means…
options: noticing it as a thought, without having to obey it
pushing it away until it stops
questions.right: That's it. You give it a bit of space instead of a fight.
questions.wrong: Not quite. Unhooking means noticing the thought as a thought. No arguing or pushing away needed.

questions.q: Dropping anchor is meant to…
options: help you stay steady while hard feelings are here
questions.right: Yes. The storm may keep going for a while, and you can stay steady in it.
questions.wrong: It's about staying steady while the feelings are here. They may not go away straight away, and that's okay.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: What thought tends to hook you most? What happens when you notice it as "just a thought"?

step.title: Drop anchor once today
step.detail: Next time feelings run high, take one minute: notice, feel your feet, look around.

sources.title: The Happiness Trap (book and program; concepts only, not reproduced)

modules.title: Riding out intense moments (DBT skills basics)
modules.summary: STOP, TIPP, opposite action and wise mind, in plain words.

cards.title: What DBT is
cards.body: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was developed by psychologist Marsha Linehan. It teaches skills for getting through intense moments and managing strong emotions. This module is a short, general introduction, not DBT therapy.

cards.title: STOP
cards.body: Stop: freeze for a moment. Take a step back and breathe. Observe what's going on inside and around you. Proceed mindfully, choosing what will help.

cards.title: TIPP
cards.body: Quick body-based skills: cool your face with cold water, do a short burst of movement, slow your breathing, and tense then relax your muscles. Skip cold water or hard exercise if you have a heart condition or other health concern, and check with your doctor.

cards.title: Opposite action
cards.body: When an emotion pushes you to do something that won't help, try gently doing the opposite. If fear says hide, take one small step forward. If shame says withdraw, reach out to one person.

cards.title: Wise mind
cards.body: DBT describes an emotion mind (feelings in charge) and a reasonable mind (logic in charge). Wise mind is where both meet, that quiet sense of what's right for you.

questions.q: In STOP, what does the O stand for?
questions.right: Yes: notice what's going on inside and around you.
questions.wrong: It's Observe: notice what's happening inside and around you.

questions.q: Fear is telling you to cancel on a friend. What would opposite action look like?
options: Go, even for a short time
questions.right: That's it. Small steps count.
questions.wrong: Opposite action would be going, even briefly. Small steps count.

questions.q: Wise mind is…
questions.right: Right.
questions.wrong: Wise mind is where feelings and reason meet, not ignoring either.

steps.title: Paced breathing
steps.intro: Slow breathing is one of the TIPP skills. Follow along for about a minute.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Which of these skills could you use in your hardest moments? What would help you remember it?

step.title: Practise STOP once today
step.detail: Use STOP in a small moment of frustration, so it's easier to reach for in a big one.

sources.title: DBT Skills Training Manual, 2nd edition (Guilford Press, 2015). Book reference, concepts only.

modules.title: Your thought record (CBT)
modules.summary: Slow a hard moment down on paper and find a more balanced view.

cards.title: Why write it down
cards.body: When a thought is in your head, it can feel like the whole truth. Writing it down helps you look at it from a little distance.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: You note the situation, the thought, and how you felt. Then you look for what supports the thought, what doesn't, and a more balanced way to see it.

cards.title: Balanced, not positive
cards.body: The aim isn't to force a happy thought. It's to find something fairer and more helpful that you can actually believe.

steps.title: Fill in a thought record
steps.intro: Take your time. You can leave any box empty. If you save it, it's kept privately on your account and encrypted.

questions.q: A balanced thought is…
options: a fairer view you can actually believe
questions.right: Yes.
questions.wrong: It's a fairer view you can believe, not a forced positive one.

questions.q: Why look for evidence against a thought?
options: To see the whole picture, not just the scary part
questions.right: Exactly. It's about seeing more of the picture.
questions.wrong: It's not about being hard on yourself. It helps you see the whole picture.

step.title: Do one thought record this week
step.detail: Next time a thought knocks you around, come back and fill one in.

sources.org: THIS WAY UP (St Vincent's Hospital Sydney)
sources.title: Learning hub

modules.title: What matters to you (ACT values and committed action)
modules.summary: Sort your values, then choose one small step guided by them.

cards.title: Values are a direction
cards.body: In ACT, values are how you want to be and what you want to stand for, like being caring or honest. They're more like a compass than a finish line.

cards.title: Goals are stops on the way
cards.body: A goal can be ticked off. A value can't, but it can guide which goals you pick and how you go about them.

cards.title: Committed action
cards.body: Committed action means taking steps guided by your values, even when hard thoughts and feelings come along for the ride.

steps.title: Sort your values
steps.intro: For each value, choose how important it feels to you right now. There are no right answers.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: Pick one value that matters most right now. What's one small thing you could do this week that fits it?

questions.q: Which of these is a value rather than a goal?
questions.right: Yes. You can keep living it, every day.
questions.wrong: Running 5 km is a goal. Looking after your health is the value behind it.

questions.q: Committed action means…
options: taking steps that matter even when it's uncomfortable
questions.right: That's it.
questions.wrong: It means taking steps that matter even with discomfort along for the ride.

step.title: Take one small step guided by a value
step.detail: Choose something that takes 10 minutes or less and fits a value you sorted as very important.

sources.title: The Happiness Trap (book and program; concepts only, not reproduced)

modules.title: Doing more of what helps (behavioural activation)
modules.summary: Break the low-mood cycle with small, planned activities.

cards.title: Doing less, feeling worse
cards.body: When mood is low, we often do less. Doing less can mean fewer good moments, which can make mood lower again.

cards.title: Action can come first
cards.body: Waiting to feel motivated can mean waiting a long time. Behavioural activation flips it: do a small thing first, and mood often follows a little.

cards.title: Two kinds of activity
cards.body: Some activities bring enjoyment (a walk, music, a cuppa with a friend). Others bring a sense of achievement (washing up, paying a bill). Both help.

cards.title: Start tiny
cards.body: Pick something so small it feels almost too easy. Plan when you'll do it. Notice how you feel after.

steps.title: Pick some activities
steps.intro: Sort these by how likely you'd be to try them this week. Nothing here is saved.
items: Have a shower and get dressed
Do one small job I've been putting off

questions.q: In behavioural activation, motivation…
questions.right: Yes. Small steps first.
questions.wrong: It often works the other way: a small action first, and motivation can follow.

questions.q: A good first step is…
options: something big to make up for lost time
questions.right: That's it.
questions.wrong: Small and planned works better than big and hard.

step.title: Plan one small activity for tomorrow
step.detail: Pick one activity, choose a time, and notice how you feel afterwards.

sources.org: THIS WAY UP (St Vincent's Hospital Sydney)
sources.title: Learning hub

modules.title: Making room for feelings (ACT acceptance)
modules.summary: Practise letting hard feelings be there, without a fight.

cards.title: Fighting feelings can backfire
cards.body: Pushing a feeling away often makes it louder, and can lead to things we regret, like drinking or using to get rid of it.

cards.title: Acceptance is not giving up
cards.body: In ACT, acceptance means letting a feeling be there for now, without liking it or wanting it. It frees up energy for what matters.

cards.title: Expansion
cards.body: Expansion is a way to practise this: notice where the feeling is, breathe around it, and give it a bit more space, like loosening a tight belt.

steps.title: Make room (about a minute)
steps.intro: Follow each prompt. If it gets too much, stop and try dropping anchor or calling someone instead.

phases.label: Find it
phases.text: Notice where in your body the feeling is strongest.

phases.label: Describe it
phases.text: Notice its edges. Is it hot or cool, heavy or light, still or moving?

phases.label: Breathe around it
phases.text: Breathe slowly, as if your breath is flowing in and around the feeling.

phases.label: Give it space
phases.text: See if you can let it be there, giving it a little more room.

phases.label: Widen out
phases.text: Notice the rest of your body too, and the room around you.

questions.q: Acceptance in ACT means…
options: letting it be there for now, without a fight
questions.right: Yes.
questions.wrong: It means letting it be there for now. You don't have to like it.

questions.q: If making room gets too much, you can…
options: stop, drop anchor or reach out
questions.right: Right. You're always in charge of the pace.
questions.wrong: You can always stop. Dropping anchor or reaching out is a good choice.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: What did you notice when you gave the feeling a little more room?

step.title: Make room for one feeling today
step.detail: When a hard feeling shows up, spend one minute noticing and breathing around it.

sources.title: The Happiness Trap (book and program; concepts only, not reproduced)

modules.title: Faith on hard days
modules.summary: For people who opted in to faith content: holding on to hope, and using help, when things are heavy.
modules.note: Optional faith layer. Faith sits alongside professional care, never instead of it.

cards.title: Hard days happen to people of faith too
cards.body: Struggling with mood, anxiety or cravings is not a sign of weak faith. Many people in the Bible were honest with God about feeling low, afraid or worn out.

cards.title: Near to the broken-hearted
cards.body: Psalm 34:18 (WEB): “Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.” Being close to God and feeling awful can happen on the same day.

cards.title: Help is part of the answer
cards.body: Prayer and practical help work together. Seeing a GP, calling a support line, talking to a counsellor or using a coping tool are good, wise steps. They are not a lack of trust.

cards.title: If you're not safe
cards.body: If you might act on thoughts of suicide or you're in danger, call 000 now, or Lifeline on 13 11 14. Your safety plan is in Get help.

questions.q: Seeing a counsellor or GP when you're a person of faith is…
options: a sign you don't trust God
a wise step that can sit alongside prayer
questions.right: Yes. Faith and good care work together.
questions.wrong: Many Christians see good care as one of the ways God helps. It's a wise step, not a failure.

questions.q: Feeling low or anxious means your faith is weak.
questions.right: That's right. Hard feelings are part of being human.
questions.wrong: Not true. People with deep faith have hard days too. You're not doing faith wrong.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: What would you like to say to God about today, honestly? You can keep this private.

step.title: Pray one honest sentence, then text one support person
step.detail: Tell God how today really is in one line. Then send one person a short message, even just ‘rough day’.

sources.title: Public domain translation used for every quoted verse

modules.title: Grace after a lapse
modules.summary: For people who opted in to faith content: shame, grace and getting back on your path after a slip.
modules.note: Optional faith layer. Faith sits alongside professional care, never instead of it.

cards.title: Shame says ‘you are the problem’
cards.body: After a lapse, shame can say you're beyond help. Grace says you're loved and can take the next step. Shame tends to push people back towards using; grace helps people get up again.

cards.title: Nothing can separate
cards.body: Romans 8:38–39 says that nothing in all creation “will be able to separate us from God’s love, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (WEB). That includes a hard week.

cards.title: Honest, then practical
cards.body: Many people find it helps to be honest with God and one trusted person, then look at their relapse plan: what happened, what helped, and one change for next time.

steps.title: A minute of stillness
steps.intro: Breathe in gently, then breathe out a little longer. If you like, on each out-breath, remember that you are still loved. Stop whenever you like.

phases.label: Breathe in
phases.text: Breathe in gently through your nose.

phases.label: Breathe out
phases.text: Breathe out slowly. You are still loved.

steps.title: Your turn (optional)
steps.prompt: What is one kind thing you can say to yourself about the lapse, and one thing you'd like to do differently?

step.title: Open my relapse plan and add one thing I learnt
step.detail: Keep it short. One line is enough.

sources.title: Public domain translation used for every quoted verse
